title: Streaming chunked attention thresholds (FlashAttention vs PagedAttention) - labnote
content:
Summary:

This note captures a focused investigation into how FlashAttention and a paged-attention fallback behave under a streaming / chunked token arrival pattern. The goal is to find the operational threshold (chunk size / inter-arrival gap / sequence hot length) where FlashAttention provides stable p99 latency and throughput benefits versus when paged attention or fused-op fallbacks become preferable. This came out of RH-2048 (incident-style spikes when streaming chat clients send short tokens intermittently).

Why this matters:
- Many customers use streaming token-by-token responses; network/SDK batching produces small chunks that arrive at varying intervals.
- Kernel selection logic currently favors FlashAttention for long steady sequences, but there are corner cases where the kernel handshake + kernel priming cost + KV cache churn causes p99 tail spikes.
- We need a practical threshold policy for the scheduler that optimizes for p99 latency without sacrificing sustained throughput for longer sequences.

Hypotheses to test:
1) When chunks are smaller than ~8 tokens with inter-arrival > 30ms, FlashAttention loses its advantage due to kernel start-up and fusion priming costs; paged attention has lower p99.
2) Enabling fused ops helps throughput but widens variance in tail latency for bursty streams because fused kernels have heavier priming.
3) KV cache eviction / page thrash increases when mixed-length sessions are colocated on the same device, amplifying FlashAttention jitter.

Hardware / baseline:
- Node: 1 x NVIDIA A100-SXM8 80GB, CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.x, nsys 23.8 used for traces.
- Runtime: runtime/v0.73 (feature: adaptive-kernel-router), all telemetry flags on.
- Model: Llama-2-7B-Chat (quantized to q4f16), 4096 context.
- Workload harness: local harness that simulates clients sending initial prompt (seed len 40) then streaming generation in chunk sizes [1,2,4,8,16,32] tokens with inter-arrival gaps [0ms, 10ms, 30ms, 100ms].
- Mixed workload: 30% long-steady (gen 512 tokens, batch coalesced), 70% streaming-chunked sessions.

Experiment matrix (selected runs):
- Variant A: FlashAttention enabled, fused-ops ON, scheduler kernel_hint=flash-first
- Variant B: PagedAttention forced, fused-ops OFF
- Variant C: FlashAttention enabled, fused-ops OFF (to separate fusion priming cost)
- Variant D: FlashAttention enabled, fused-ops ON, eviction-threshold low (aggressive KV eviction)

Profiler commands (representative):
- nsys profile --sample=none -o runA.ns --trace=cuda,osrt --capture-range=nvtx ./harness --config streaming-A.json
- nvprof style counters (kernel timings exported to CSV) via the internal perf exporter.

Key metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 generation step latency (ms), tokens/sec sustained, kernel call counts, kernel handoff occurrences, KV eviction counts per minute, GPU SM utilization distribution.

Representative findings (abridged):
1) Single-session microbench (no colocation):
- Chunk=1, gap=30ms: Variant A p99=120ms, p95=70ms, tokens/sec=90; Variant B p99=55ms, p95=40ms, tokens/sec=60. Interpretation: Flash attention has higher p99 for isolated, very small chunks because kernel handshake + small-batch inefficiency dominates; paged path is cheaper for tiny isolated steps.
- Chunk=8, gap=10ms: Variant A p99=45ms, p95=30ms, tokens/sec=260; Variant B p99=78ms, p95=55ms, tokens/sec=180. Interpretation: Flash wins once chunk >= ~6-8 tokens and arrival gap is small enough to let batching/coalescing happen.

2) Mixed-workload multi-session (colocation):
- With fusion ON (Variant A), we observed occasional p99 spikes up to 320ms when short streaming sessions collided with long steady sessions. Kernel handoff logs show up to 3 rapid kernel switches across the same stream (flash->paged->flash) due to scheduler heuristics responding to transient pressure. KV eviction rate rose by 4x during these micro-jams.
- With fusion OFF (Variant C), p99 spikes reduced (max ~180ms), but sustained tokens/sec dropped ~12% for long sessions.
- Forcing paged path (Variant B) flattened p99 (max 120ms) but reduced tokens/sec for heavy long jobs by 25%.

3) Effect of inter-arrival gap:
- Gaps >50ms consistently favor paged path for chunk sizes <=4. Below 20ms with chunk >=4, flash tends to be better.

4) Fused ops priming cost characterization:
- Fused kernels have a one-time priming cost (~8-12ms) and higher register / shared memory setup. For high-frequency short bursts, the accumulate priming cost becomes visible in p99.
- When fused ops are present but the request mix is homogeneous long sequences, they are net-positive: +30% tokens/sec.

Telemetry traces and examples (text excerpts):
- Trace A (Flash, chunk=1, gap=30ms): NVTX notes show kernel_launch[flash_attention] (1.2ms) + kernel_handshake(6.8ms) + aten_fused_preload(3.9ms) before actual compute, cumulatively adding ~12ms overhead per step.
- Trace B (Paged, chunk=1, gap=30ms): paged_attention_compute(5.1ms) with minimal handshake.

Observed scheduler behavior and weak points:
- The kernel router aggressively switches to Flash when it sees a running seqlen > 64 in the recent window. However for streaming sessions that slowly grow beyond 64 over multiple small chunks, this causes repeated switch costs.
- The router window is short (500ms) and threshold clamps too low for streaming patterns.
- KV cache eviction is tied to kernel variant state; switching variant causes reallocation pressures and page-table churn.

Operational recommendation (short term):
1) Introduce a "streaming-holdoff" for kernel switching: if a session produces chunks <=4 tokens with inter-arrival >25ms for the first N steps, bias to paged until a steady-state observation window (e.g., 256 tokens or sustained <20ms gap).
2) Add a lightweight priming cache: pre-warm fused kernels only when we detect a high-confidence long sequence (heuristic: predicted remaining tokens > 64 from generation policy).
3) Expose a per-route config option in Console to set conservative kernel policy for low-latency streaming endpoints (default: streaming-optimized).

Longer-term investigations (follow-ups):
- Explore a low-cost micro-batching layer at the SDK that queues up to X ms to coalesce small chunks (trade client latency vs server p99).
- Quantify hybrid kernels that keep handshake small: micro-fused ops that split priming into a cheap fast-path and an optimized slow-path.
- Assess impact on memory fragmentation if we pin streaming sessions to separate GPU partitions (colocation isolation).

Experiment artifacts and commands to reproduce locally:
- harness config dir: ./harness/configs/streaming-experiments/ (see linked PR for exact JSON).
- Example command: ./harness/run_streaming --model llama-2-7b-chat --chunks 1,2,4,8 --gaps 0,10,30,100 --variant flash-fused
- Perf exporter output: /tmp/perf-run-STREAM-A.csv (kernels, durations, timestamps).

Open questions & notes to reviewers:
- We need to validate these findings on at least two more hardware families (H100, L40s) because kernel priming ratios change with SM count and micro-architectural differences.
- Confirm whether quantization format (q4f16 vs q8) materially changes handshake cost. Preliminary quick-check shows small effect but needs systematic sweep.
- Is a default conservative policy acceptable for PLG-hosted API, or should we make it route-specific only? Expect product input.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Priya: Draft kernel router patch to add streaming-holdoff flag and unit tests (due 2025-02-25).
- Alex: Run same matrix on H100 cluster (node h100-cluster-2) and upload traces (due 2025-02-21).
- Marco: Prototype SDK micro-coalescer to batch short chunks for 10ms windows; add metrics to measure end-to-end client latency impact (due 2025-03-04).

Appendix: Quick numeric summary table (representative single-node mixed workload)
- Variant A (Flash+fused): p50=18ms, p95=64ms, p99=210ms, tokens/sec=720
- Variant B (Paged only): p50=22ms, p95=58ms, p99=110ms, tokens/sec=520
- Variant C (Flash, fused OFF): p50=20ms, p95=62ms, p99=150ms, tokens/sec=630

Notes: Table above is synthetic aggregate of the runs described; exact CSVs are in linked artifacts.
